Abstract:
The clinical translations of drugs and nanomedicines depend on coherent pharmaceutical research based on biologically accurate screening approaches. Since establishing the 2D in vitro cell culture method, the scientific community has improved cell‐based drug screening assays and models. Those advances result in more informative biochemical assays and the development of 3D multicellular models to describe the biological complexity better and enhance the simulation of the in vivo microenvironment. Despite the overall dominance of conventional 2D and 3D cell macroscopic culture methods, they present physicochemical and operational challenges that impair the scale‐up of drug screening by not allowing a high parallelization, multidrug combination, and high‐throughput screening. Their combination and complementarity with microfluidic platforms enable the development of microfluidics‐based cell culture platforms with unequivocal advantages in drug screening and cell therapies. Thus, this review presents an updated and consolidated view of cell culture miniaturization's physical, chemical, and operational considerations in the pharmaceutical research scenario. It clarifies advances in the field using gradient‐based microfluidics, droplet‐based microfluidics, printed‐based microfluidics, digital‐based microfluidics, SlipChip, and paper‐based microfluidics. Finally, it presents a comparative analysis of the performance of cell‐based methods in life research and development to achieve increased precision in the drug screening process.

Abstract:
Digital microfluidics has emerged as a promising platform for cell culture, offering precise control over droplet-based microenvironments while enabling automation and miniaturization. This review examines the integration of DMF with various cell culture substrates, including hydrogels and synthetic polymers, and evaluates their advantages and limitations for supporting cellular growth, adhesion, and viability. The influence of AC and DC actuation modes on droplet handling, as well as their effects on cell behavior, are also discussed. I elaborate how DMF systems can be designed to deliver and modulate physical and biochemical stimuli, such as shear stress, temperature, and gradients of signaling molecules, to better mimic in vivo conditions and study cell behavior in dynamic environments. Next, I highlight the incorporation of analytical tools and sorting techniques in DMF-based cell culture and explore its potential applications in organ-on-chip systems. While DMF presents unique opportunities for cell-based research, challenges such as material compatibility, cell viability, and system stability remain. This review provides a critical assessment of current developments and future directions for DMF in cell culture applications.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This review deals with the development and progress of micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) actuators, which are needed in microfluidic applications, such as lab-on-a-chip and diagnostics. In the last 10 years, there have been tremendous advances in materials, microfabrication and computational modeling that have increased the functionality and scope of MEMS-based microfluidic actuation. This study classifies MEMS actuators on the basis of the physical method of actuation, including electrostatic, piezoelectric, and pneumatic actuation designs, in comparison with their application in pumping, valving, and droplet control. It examines the suitability of emerging structural and functional materials, such as piezoelectric thin-films and electroactive polymers, paying special attention to their reliability and biocompatibility. It also highlights the progress in multiphysics modeling that incorporates electrical, thermal, mechanical, and fluidic models, which facilitates the efficient design and performance optimization procedures. Other trends are multifunctional actuators with built-in sensing capability and the use of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted design in production. With these developments, however, there exist issues of power efficiency, thermal control, fabrication uniformity and operational durability, and also the absence of standardized benchmarking. Finally, future research directions are outlined, including hybrid MEMS actuation, intelligent microfluidic operations, to improve the performance of the system and enable the transfer of the lab demonstrations to the large scale application of the system.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Multiwell plates are prominent in the biological and chemical sciences; however, they face limitations in terms of throughput and deployment in emerging bioengineering fields. Droplet microarrays, as an open microfluidic technology, organise tiny droplets typically in the order of thousands, on an accessible plate. In this perspective, we summarise current approaches for generating droplets, fluid handling on them, and analysis within droplet microarrays. By enabling unique plate engineering opportunities, demonstrating the necessary experimental procedures required for manipulating and interacting with biological cells, and integrating with label-free analytical techniques, droplet microarrays can be deployed across a more extensive experimental domain than what is currently covered by multiwell plates. Droplet microarrays thus offer a solution to the bottlenecks associated with multiwell plates, particularly in the areas of biological cultivation and high-throughput compound screening.

Abstract:
Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting has become mainstream for precise and repeatable high-throughput fabrication of complex cell cultures and tissue constructs in drug testing and regenerative medicine, food products, dental and medical implants, biosensors, and so forth. Due to this tremendous growth in demand, an overwhelming amount of hardware manufacturers have recently flooded the market with different types of low-cost bioprinter models—a price segment that is most affordable to typical-sized laboratories. These machines range in sophistication, type of the underlying printing technology, and possible add-ons/features, which makes the selection process rather daunting (especially for a nonexpert customer). Yet, the review articles available in the literature mostly focus on the technical aspects of the printer technologies under development, as opposed to explaining the differences in what is already on the market. In contrast, this paper provides a snapshot of the fast-evolving low-cost bioprinter niche, as well as reputation profiles (relevant to delivery time, part quality, adherence to specifications, warranty, maintenance, etc.) of the companies selling these machines. Specifically, models spanning three dominant technologies—microextrusion, droplet-based/inkjet, and light-based/crosslinking—are reviewed. Additionally, representative examples of high-end competitors (including up-and-coming microfluidics-based bioprinters) are discussed to highlight their major differences and advantages relative to the low-cost models. Finally, forecasts are made based on the trends observed during this survey, as to the anticipated trickling down of the high-end technologies to the low-cost printers. Overall, this paper provides insight for guiding buyers on a limited budget toward making informed purchasing decisions in this fast-paced market.

Abstract:
3D bioprinting enables fabrication of cell-laden bioinks into complex, biomimetic tissues. However, achieving the spatial and functional heterogeneity of native tissues still poses significant challenges. Microfluidics has emerged as a complementary technology, offering precise control over material flow, mixing, and deposition at the microscale. This review highlights the integration of microfluidics with 3D bioprinting, with a particular focus on the development of advanced “printhead-on-a-chip” systems that enable real-time material switching, gradient formation, and enhanced resolution among other functionalities. Innovations across extrusion, coaxial, droplet-based, light-based, and voxel-based bioprinting modalities are explored, showcasing the transformative potential of microfluidics in creating multifunctional and heterogeneous tissue architectures. Applications in tissue heterogeneity, vascularization, tumor microenvironments, microfiber cellular technology, and organ-on-a-chip systems are discussed, underscoring microfluidics’ role in advancing tissue engineering, disease modeling, and drug discovery. Future directions outline the need for scalability, standardization, and simplified workflows that enhance accessibility for broader adoption of microfluidic bioprinting.

Abstract:
Numerous cancer-associated deaths are owing to a lack of effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. Microfluidic systems for analyzing a low volume of samples offer a precise, quick, and user-friendly technique for cancer diagnosis and treatment. Microfluidic devices can detect many cancer-diagnostic factors from biological fluids and also generate appropriate nanoparticles for drug delivery. Thus, microfluidics may be valuable in the cancer field due to its high sensitivity, high throughput, and low cost. In the present article, we aim to review recent achievements in the application of microfluidic systems for the diagnosis and treatment of various cancers. Abstract:
The integration of three-dimensional (3D) printing techniques into the domains of biomedical research and personalized medicine highlights the evolving paradigm shifts within contemporary healthcare. This technological advancement signifies potential breakthroughs in patient-specific therapeutic interventions and innovations. This systematic review offers a critical assessment of the existing literature, elucidating the present status, inherent challenges, and prospective avenues of 3D printing in augmenting biomedical applications and formulating tailored medical strategies. Based on an exhaustive literature analysis comprising empirical studies, case studies, and extensive reviews from the past decade, pivotal sectors including tissue engineering, prosthetic development, drug delivery systems, and customized medical apparatuses are delineated. The advent of 3D printing provides precision in the fabrication of patient-centric implants, bio-structures, and devices, thereby mitigating associated risks. Concurrently, it facilitates the ideation of individualized drug delivery paradigms to optimize therapeutic outcomes. Notwithstanding these advancements, issues concerning material biocompatibility, regulatory compliance, and the economic implications of avant-garde printing techniques persist. To fully harness the transformative potential of 3D printing in healthcare, collaborative endeavors amongst academicians, clinicians, industrial entities, and regulatory bodies are paramount. With continued research and innovation, 3D printing is poised to redefine the trajectories of biomedical science and patient-centric care. The paper aims to justify the research objective of whether to what extent the integration of 3D printing technology in biomedicine enhances patient-specific treatment and contributes to improved healthcare outcomes.

Abstract:
The fabrication of microfluidic devices has progressed from cleanroom manufacturing to replica molding in polymers, and more recently to direct manufacturing by subtractive (e.g., laser machining) and additive (e.g., 3D printing) techniques, notably digital light processing (DLP) photopolymerization. However, many methods require technical expertise and DLP 3D printers remain expensive at a cost ∼15-30 K USD with ∼8 M pixels that are 25-40 μm in size. Here, we introduce (i) the use of low-cost (∼150-600 USD) liquid crystal display (LCD) photopolymerization 3D printing with ∼8-58 M pixels that are 18-35 μm in size for direct microfluidic device fabrication, and (ii) a poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate-based ink developed for LCD 3D printing (PLInk). We optimized PLInk for high resolution, fast 3D printing and biocompatibility while considering the illumination inhomogeneity and low power density of LCD 3D printers. We made lateral features as small as 75 μm, 22 μm-thick embedded membranes, and circular channels with a 110 μm radius. We 3D printed microfluidic devices previously manufactured by other methods, including an embedded 3D micromixer, a membrane microvalve, and an autonomous capillaric circuit (CC) deployed for interferon-γ detection with excellent performance (limit of detection: 12 pg mL-1, CV: 6.8%). We made PLInk-based organ-on-a-chip devices in 384-well plate format and produced 3420 individual devices within an 8 h print run. We used the devices to co-culture two spheroids separated by a vascular barrier over 5 days and observed endothelial sprouting, cellular reorganization, and migration. LCD 3D printing together with tailored inks pave the way for democratizing access to high-resolution manufacturing of ready-to-use microfluidic and organ-on-a-chip devices by anyone, anywhere.

From text 'lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 3-6'.

Pascal Miéville, Adam Lisowski, Henryk Zolnowski, Keyan Villat, Alec Schmidt, Edy Mariano, Jean-Charles Cousty, Jérôme Guérin, Ashley Stark, Frédéric Vasserot, Achim Ammon, David Gueller, Florian Nanteuil, Jean-Jacques Schwartz, Mathias Cherbuin, Marc Kunze, and Giuseppe Costanzo. This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes STORMS as a stochastic, vacuum-assisted coring and glass-encapsulation workflow intended to decouple solid sampling from synthesis. It states that pre-calibrated sampling generates individually laser-sealed capsules, which are stored and later selected by a combinatorial matching algorithm before being broken over reaction vessels. The claimed demonstrated operating range is 0.1–20 mg across diverse solids, while the detailed calibration discussion reports two ranges, 0.1–1 mg and 1–8–10 mg, with the upper limit material-dependent and determined by the onset of nonlinearity. The method removes intermediate feedback weighing: only the empty-capsule and final capsule measurements are required. Dispensing variability is characterized using Gaussian distributions and linear regression; predefined tolerances are compensated during later liquid handling, including reagents, solutions, and solvents. This supports investigation of whether solvent volumes are adjusted to measured mass, but the excerpt does not specify the exact adjustment algorithm or provide numerical on-target error data. It also does not discuss hardware openness versus software, Miau’s $900 component-cost claim or validation at 1–5 mg, nor Winkler 2022 drug-stock loading details. The figures are referenced but not provided as usable images here.

The excerpt provides direct evidence that STORMS was engineered for automated solid coring across the 1–5 mg range: the specified 1.5 mm coring tube covers the broader 1–10 mg range, while the 0.6 mm tube covers 0.1–1 mg. Dispensed mass is controlled by the adjustable rod position, with vacuum assistance intended to improve filling reproducibility across powders and wax-like solids. Hardware details include interchangeable stainless-steel tubes and rods, robotic vial positioning, capsule dispensing, enclosed CO₂ laser sealing, and robotic capsule pick-and-place/crushing. Software is represented by calibration datasets, experimental mass tables, effective capsule distributions, and a rule-based matching algorithm that selects capsule combinations within a specified tolerance. Capsules are weighed after filling, so the system records the exact solid mass before storage and later reaction-plate assembly. However, this excerpt does not provide numerical on-target error, accuracy, or precision results for 1–5 mg dispensing, nor does it establish that solvent volume is automatically adjusted to measured mass. It also contains no information about Miau’s claimed $900 component cost or validation at 1–5 mg, and no details about Winkler 2022 drug-stock loading or a prospective minimal-fluidic chip.

## pqac-00000033

This article has 0 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt provides primary calibration and workflow evidence for STORMS, especially for milligram-scale capsule coring. Using a 1.5 mm vacuum-assisted coring tool, the authors report a linear relationship between rod height and dispensed mass across most tested powders; the 3–5 mg range is specifically favored by the matching algorithm to reduce relative balance uncertainty. For Inhalac 70, repeated measurements showed linear behavior from 1–6 mm rod height with R² = 0.9997, while dispersion remained stable throughout that range. The text attributes final precision to analytical-balance readability and repeatability, rather than describing a separate on-target error metric in the excerpt. It also states that vacuum-assisted sampling can broaden compatibility, particularly for larger particles and higher Carr-index powders. STORMS is described as an architecture combining pre-calibration, stochastic sampling, encapsulation, and algorithmic matching; the excerpt emphasizes workflow/software decoupling rather than hardware openness. Handling time is reported as 20–30 seconds per capsule versus approximately two minutes for deterministic dispensing, with substantial plate-level time reductions. No information here establishes automated solvent-volume adjustment based on measured capsule mass. The excerpt contains no data about Miau’s $900 component-cost claim or 1–5 mg validation, and no details about Winkler 2022 drug-stock loading for a prospective fluidic chip.

A two-day workshop activity is described in which postgraduate students are introduced to (i) the theory and application of Design-of-Experiments (DOE) approaches and (ii) the implementation of affordable automation technologies and related data analysis of a system of catalytic interest. This work involved the design and delivery of a short lecture to introduce the theory of DOE followed by practical demonstrations of the application of automation technologies. Specifically, a fractional factorial design was used to interrogate the input space—base, solvent, temperature, time—of the Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling (SMCC) of para-bromoanisole and para-fluorophenylboronic acid using automated solid and liquid handling robots and online HPLC analysis. This was supplemented by a second lecture following data acquisition in which the collected HPLC data was analyzed. The workshop was delivered to a cohort of 15 students at the postgraduate level. Pleasingly, students demonstrated a high degree of engagement with this course structure and reported an increased theoretical understanding of DOE approaches to reaction optimization.

Abstract:
Newer solid‐phase peptide synthesis and release strategies enable the production of short peptides with high purity, allowing direct screening for desired bioactivity without prior chromatographic purification. However, the maximum number of peptides that can currently be synthesized per microplate reactor is 96, allowing the parallel synthesis of 384 peptides in modern devices that have space for 4 microplate reactors. To synthesize larger numbers of peptides, we modified a commercially available peptide synthesizer to enable the production of peptides in 384‐well plates, which allows the synthesis of 1,536 peptides in one run (4 × 384 peptides). We report new hardware components and customized software that allowed for the synthesis of 1,536 short peptides in good quantity (average > 0.5 μmol), at high concentration (average > 10 mM), and decent purity without purification (average > 80%). The high‐throughput peptide synthesis, which we developed with peptide drug development in mind, may be widely used for peptide library synthesis and screening, antibody epitope scanning, epitope mimetic development, or protease/kinase substrate screening.

Abstract:
<jats:p>This review proposes the concept of a “frugal twin,” similar to a digital twin, but for physical experiments. Frugal twins range from simple toy examples to low-cost surrogates of high-cost research. For example, a color-mixing self-driving laboratory (SDL) is a low-cost version of a costly multi-step chemical discovery SDL. We need frugal twins because they provide hands-on experience, a test bed for software prototyping (e.g., optimization, data infrastructure), and a low barrier to entry for democratizing SDLs. However, there is room for improvement. The true value of frugal twins can be realized in three core areas. Firstly, hardware and software modularity, secondly, purpose-built design (human-inspired vs. hardware-centric vs. human-in-the-loop), and thirdly state-of-the-art (SOTA) software (e.g., multi-fidelity optimization). We also describe the ethical benefits and risks that come with the democratization of science through frugal twins. In future work, we suggest ideas for new frugal twins, SDL educational course outcomes, and a classification scheme for autonomy levels.</jats:p>

High-Throughput Screening for Drug Combinations

Paul Shinn, Lu Chen, Marc Ferrer, Zina Itkin, Carleen Klumpp-Thomas,
Crystal McKnight, Sam Michael, Tim Mierzwa, Craig Thomas,
Kelli Wilson, and Rajarshi Guha



Abstract

The identiﬁcation of drug combinations as alternatives to single-agent therapeutics has traditionally been a
slow, largely manual process. In the last 10 years, high-throughput screening platforms have been devel-
oped that enable routine screening of thousands of drug pairs in an in vitro setting. In this chapter, we
describe the workﬂow involved in screening a single agent versus a library of mechanistically annotated,
investigation, and approved drugs using a full dose-response matrix scheme using viability as the readout.
We provide details of the automation required to run the screen and the informatics required to process data
from screening robot and subsequent analysis and visualization of the datasets.

   Key words Drug combination screening, Acoustic dispensing, Automation, Compound manage-
    ment, Synergy


1  Introduction

                    High-throughput screening for compounds that affect cell viability
                       has been utilized as a method for discovery of novel treatments for
                        various human diseases. For patients with cancer and certain infec-
                         tious diseases, combinations of drugs are given to achieve maximal
                            clinical beneﬁt. An additional beneﬁt of a clinically synergistic drug
                     combination is that both drugs may be synergistic at a low dose,
                    which can reduce off target toxicities. For infectious diseases such as
                   HIV, drug combinations are critical to prevent infectious agents
                    from acquiring mutations to evade the action of a single drug. The
                        search for novel synergistic drug pairs requires the development of a
                         systematic, large-scale screening platform. CombinatoRX, a bio-
                       tech company acquired in 2014 by Horizon Discovery, was the ﬁrst
                       to publish a series of papers utilizing drug combination screening to
                       explore synergistic drug responses in various disease models such as
                       cancer and drug-resistant bacteria [1–3]. A recent study spear-
                    headed  by   AstraZeneca  and  NCI-DREAM   utilized   a



Richard S. Larson and Tudor I. Oprea (eds.), Bioinformatics and Drug Discovery, Methods in Molecular Biology, vol. 1939,
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4939-9089-4_2, © Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2019
                                1112      Paul Shinn et al.


                     crowdsourcing approach to predict synergistic drug combinations
                         for treatment of B-cell lymphoma [4].
                     The development of a methodology for large-scale testing of
                    drug combinations in vitro was advanced by the incorporation of
                        acoustic dispensing technology, which allows for the ﬂexibility of an
                     anywhere-to-anywhere compound transfer. Given that drug com-
                       bination screening requires two or more compounds present in a
                         single well, contact-based transfer methods would be costly in time
                    and resources to reduce the possibility of contamination between
                          transfer steps. Using a noncontact dispenser greatly reduces the
                   amount of sample and consumables used as well as the complexity
                        that would be involved if traditional contact-based pipetting had
                    been applied.
                      Here we report the methods and workﬂow speciﬁcally for drug
                     combination screening that has been implemented and optimized
                          at the National Institutes of Health’s National Center for Advanc-
                       ing  Translational  Sciences (NCATS). This drug combination
                       screening platform has been applied to multiple areas of drug
                       discovery including cancer, malaria, Ebola, and various other dis-
                        ease models [5–8] and as of 2016 has tested over 200,000 discrete
                    drug  combinations.  This  automated  screening  platform  has
                       required the use of in-house software development as well as inte-
                       gration of various instrumentations in order to achieve an almost
                            fully automated workﬂow. We typically refer to this as Matrix
                        screening, due to the layout of the drug combinations in a grid
                      format on the ﬁnal plate. The workﬂow presented here was utilized
                         for screening of the Ewing’s sarcoma  cell  line and has been
                      published [8].

                                                            Available online 14 December 2007



Abstract

  As the number of pharmaceutical candidate compounds increases, so does the need for development workﬂow that is capable of handling more
compounds in shorter times. In this paper, the establishment of a high-throughput automated powder compatibility testing system is reported.
The integrated robotic system automatically dispenses, weighs, and stores powder samples, and extracts and analyses drug substance using ultra-
performance liquid chromatography (UPLC). Although automation of powder testing systems is generally accompanied by difﬁculties in accuracy
and precision, mass tracking at every unit operation allowed the system to be validated. In a standard procedure, drug substance and an excipient
were dispensed 1:1 (w/w), stored at 70 ◦C for 9 days, dissolved in solvents, and analyzed to examine the degradation of drug substance and the
increases in related substances. The robot quantitatively discriminate between initial conditions of the incompatible powder mixtures of aspirin
and magnesium stearate (Mg-St) prepared with or without the use of a whisk and shaker system, demonstrating the capability for evaluating
powder mixtures with varying degrees of homogeneity where the contact area between excipient and drug substance differs. Differential scanning
calorimetry (DSC), however, did not clearly distinguish between those powder samples, indicating that DSC is less sensitive to powder conditions.
The incompatibility results of aspirin and Mg-St were comparable to those reported previously, demonstrating that the automated testing system is
reliable. The robot reduced manual work to one sixth and cut down on the costs of outsourcing. An extensive impact is anticipated on development
workﬂows because this system is applicable not only to compatibility testing but also to analytical method development for drug products.

## Context ID: pqac-00000051

Figure 1 illustrates the automated solid dispensing workflow using an ABB YuMi dual-arm robot. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000032)

| Published example | What was demonstrated | Where it falls short of the proposed system |
|---|---|---|
| **Astellas Powdernium/XCM, 2008 — closest match for the 5-mg preparation step.** | A commercial robot dispensed and weighed drug and excipient into glass vials; its companion workstation added solvent, stirred, filtered, diluted and tracked mass. One experiment dispensed **5 mg of an in-house compound into a 2-mL vial**, then used **1–1.5 mL solvent**. | This was a pharmaceutical compatibility/analytical workflow ending in **UPLC**, not acoustic dispensing or chip screening. Vial racks were transferred manually, and the cited 5-mg experiments specify **manual vortex mixing** before storage; it is not a fully unattended example or a low-cost/open-source build. (pqac-00000048, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000049) |
| **Queensland Compound Library, described in 2014 — closest connection to acoustic screening.** | Barcoded samples were tracked from an **automated weighing station**, dissolved in dry DMSO, and subsequently transferred by an **acoustic dispenser** into screening microplates. | The description does not establish a **1–5 mg** dose, identify an inexpensive/open-source weighing mechanism, or explicitly say that **solvent addition and mixing** were automated. The endpoint was screening plates, not an organ-on-chip. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021) |
| **STORMS, 2026 — closest disclosed milligram-scale solid-handling architecture.** | Robotic **vacuum-assisted coring** fills individually weighed, sealable glass capsules. Its milligram coring tool covers approximately **1–10 mg**, and the authors highlight **3–5 mg** portions; calibration and capsule-selection software are publicly referenced. Capsules can subsequently be opened over reaction vessels. | It uses a robot, balance and laser-sealing apparatus; **open software is not evidence of low-cost or entirely open hardware**. The reported work does not demonstrate DMSO stock preparation followed by acoustic dispensing or biological chip screening. It is coring, not an auger, vibratory or tapping feeder. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000032) |
| **Miau Microbalance Autosampler — inexpensive solid-handling precedent.** | A review lists a roughly **US$900**, 3D-printed pick-and-place device that transfers tin capsules and powder for **sub-milligram** analytical samples. | Its documented application is elemental/isotope sample preparation; the reviewed description does **not validate 1–5 mg drug dosing**, solvent addition, or downstream screening. Its original *HardwareX* paper was not available for direct verification in this search. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000011) |
| **Dual-arm biomimetic dispenser, 2023 — reusable robot-controlled weighing.** | Published code accompanies an ABB YuMi robot that manipulates spatulas, vials and a balance; its illustrated sequence shows solid delivery into vials. | Its stated **minimum dose is 20 ± 2 mg**: the **2 mg is a tolerance around 20 mg, not evidence of a 2-mg target**. The authors call it relatively inexpensive compared with commercial systems but give no demonstrated 1–5 mg drug-stock-to-screen workflow. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000051) |

**What happens downstream is well established, but usually starts with an already prepared stock.** In an NCATS drug-combination-screening protocol, investigators first *weighed compound into a tube* to make **800 µL of 10 mM DMSO stock**, vortexed and checked dissolution; automation then prepared acoustic source plates and used an ATS-100 dispenser. That is a direct precedent for the liquid-screening half, **not automated initial powder weighing**. Separately, an Echo 550 cell-screening study dispensed **2.5–100 nL** from DMSO source plates. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000044)

Actual dispensed mass—not just the requested mass—should determine solvent volume; dissolution, precipitation after aqueous dilution, and compatibility with the destination assay need checking. For scale, **1 mg of a 500 g/mol compound requires 200 µL solvent for a nominal 10 mM stock**, while 5 mg requires 1 mL; this is a calculation, not a claim that any cited dispenser validated those stocks. The Astellas study illustrates why mass tracking matters: at its 5-mg validation point, mass-corrected recovery was **100.9%** versus **108.1%** without correction. (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000062)

| **Queensland Compound Library, described in 2014 — closest connection to acoustic screening.** | Barcoded samples were tracked from an **automated weighing station**, dissolved in dry DMSO, and subsequently transferred by an **acoustic dispenser** into screening microplates. | The description does not establish a **1–5 mg** dose, identify an inexpensive/open-source weighing mechanism, or explicitly say that **solvent addition and mixing** were automated. The endpoint was screening plates, not an organ-on-chip. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021) |
| **STORMS, 2026 — closest disclosed milligram-scale solid-handling architecture.** | Robotic **vacuum-assisted coring** fills individually weighed, sealable glass capsules. Its milligram coring tool covers approximately **1–10 mg**, and the authors highlight **3–5 mg** portions; calibration and capsule-selection software are publicly referenced. Capsules can subsequently be opened over reaction vessels. | It uses a robot, balance and laser-sealing apparatus; **open software is not evidence of low-cost or entirely open hardware**. The reported work does not demonstrate DMSO stock preparation followed by acoustic dispensing or biological chip screening. It is coring, not an auger, vibratory or tapping feeder. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000032) |
| **Miau Microbalance Autosampler — inexpensive solid-handling precedent.** | A review lists a roughly **US$900**, 3D-printed pick-and-place device that transfers tin capsules and powder for **sub-milligram** analytical samples. | Its documented application is elemental/isotope sample preparation; the reviewed description does **not validate 1–5 mg drug dosing**, solvent addition, or downstream screening. Its original *HardwareX* paper was not available for direct verification in this search. (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000011) |
| **Dual-arm biomimetic dispenser, 2023 — reusable robot-controlled weighing.** | Published code accompanies an ABB YuMi robot that manipulates spatulas, vials and a balance; its illustrated sequence shows solid delivery into vials. | Its stated **minimum dose is 20 ± 2 mg**: the **2 mg is a tolerance around 20 mg, not evidence of a 2-mg target**. The authors call it relatively inexpensive compared with commercial systems but give no demonstrated 1–5 mg drug-stock-to-screen workflow. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000051) |

**What happens downstream is well established, but usually starts with an already prepared stock.** In an NCATS drug-combination-screening protocol, investigators first *weighed compound into a tube* to make **800 µL of 10 mM DMSO stock**, vortexed and checked dissolution; automation then prepared acoustic source plates and used an ATS-100 dispenser. That is a direct precedent for the liquid-screening half, **not automated initial powder weighing**. Separately, an Echo 550 cell-screening study dispensed **2.5–100 nL** from DMSO source plates. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000044)

**For a microfluidic endpoint**, a relatively low-cost, 3D-printed, Raspberry-Pi-controlled valve/micromixer has delivered premade camptothecin solutions to cell-culture wells for an IC₅₀ assay. Its demonstrated cells were in a **conventional plate**, not an organ cultured on-chip; powder-to-stock preparation was not automated. A human Liver-Chip study similarly prepared drug stocks from weighed powder or vendor vials and diluted them into perfusion medium, but did not report automated powder dispensing. Its reference to an “ECHO” instrument means an **imaging microscope**, not an Echo acoustic dispenser. (pqac-00000030, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000064, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000024)

**Practical interpretation.** The proposed integration is technically plausible, but its missing demonstration is the *validated interface* between an affordable 1–5 mg powder dispenser and automated, concentration-controlled stock production. Actual dispensed mass—not just the requested mass—should determine solvent volume; dissolution, precipitation after aqueous dilution, and compatibility with the destination assay need checking. For scale, **1 mg of a 500 g/mol compound requires 200 µL solvent for a nominal 10 mM stock**, while 5 mg requires 1 mL; this is a calculation, not a claim that any cited dispenser validated those stocks. The Astellas study illustrates why mass tracking matters: at its 5-mg validation point, mass-corrected recovery was **100.9%** versus **108.1%** without correction. (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000062)

**Bottom line:** *Yes* to automated ~5-mg drug dispensing followed by solvent processing, and *yes* to automated weighing followed eventually by acoustic screening **as separate published precedents**. *No verified example found* of their requested **low-cost/open-source, 1–5 mg, fully connected powder-to-stock-to-nanoliter-dispenser or organ-chip implementation**. (pqac-00000039, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000032)

contexts.context: The excerpt experimentally documents STORMS (stochastic robotic automation), an automated powder-sampling platform using vacuum-assisted coring tools rather than an auger or vibration dispenser. It operates in both sub-milligram and milligram regimes; the matching algorithm preferentially targets 3–5 mg masses, directly overlapping the requested approximately 1–5 mg range. The milligram tool uses a 1.5 mm coring tube and powder contained in a vessel, while a 0.6 mm inner-diameter tool addresses sub-milligram sampling. Calibration establishes a linear relationship between rod height and dispensed mass, with dispersion remaining constant across the linear range. For Inhalac 70, the reported linear interval was 1–6 mm of rod height with R² = 0.9997. Precision is assessed by final weighing and is primarily limited by analytical-balance readability and repeatability; the cited effective repeatability is 0.2 mg under operating conditions. Sampling takes 20–30 seconds per capsule, and stochastic population substantially reduces plate-preparation time. However, this excerpt provides no pricing, open-source hardware/software files, or evidence of automated solvent addition, drug-stock preparation, or vial-specific dispensing. It therefore supports STORMS as an experimentally demonstrated gravimetric/coring-based automated solid dispenser, but not the requested open-source or low-cost classification.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes STORMS, an experimentally demonstrated automated solid microsampling and dispensing platform capable of preparing approximately milligram-scale solid samples for reaction vials or plates. Its dispenser is neither an auger nor a vibration/tapping feeder: it uses vacuum-assisted coring. A stainless-steel external tube penetrates a powder bed, while an adjustable internal rod sets the chamber height and therefore the dispensed volume/mass. Two tube diameters cover nominal ranges of 0.1–1 mg and 1–10 mg. Vacuum applied through a calibrated tube–rod gap improves filling for fine powders and wax-like materials. The collected solid is ejected into small glass capsules, which are weighed after dispensing, laser-sealed, stored in 384-well SBS plates, and later selected algorithmically to meet target masses and tolerance constraints. A UR3 six-axis robot handles vials, capsules, and crushing; a pneumatic gripper and pincer release capsule contents into reaction vials. The excerpt reports a capsule laser-sealing success rate above 99%, but it does not provide dispensing precision/accuracy results, purchase price, bill of materials, open-source CAD/software files, or evidence of automated solvent addition or preparation of drug stocks. contexts.context: The excerpt documents an experimentally implemented automated microdispensing workflow that is relevant to approximately 1–5 mg powder dosing, although its calibration range is broader (1–9 mg). The calibration-and-dispensing software repeatedly dispenses multiple masses, averages the results to reduce noise and uncertainty, identifies the near-linear operating range, and fits a polynomial relating dispense volume to delivered mass. The calibration coefficients are stored in a SQLite database and used to invert the model for target-mass dispensing. A chemist supplies a target mass, and the system can divide that target among multiple capsules, repeating dispensing and measurement until the desired tolerance is reached. The software is openly referenced through the GitHub repository “swisscatplus/DC_Sampler.” The excerpt does not identify the physical dispenser mechanism (such as auger, vibration, tapping, or gravimetric dosing), provide purchase price or build cost, report numerical precision/tolerance, or describe open hardware/CAD files. It also does not mention automated solvent addition, preparation of drug stocks, or dispensing into multiwell plates; the surrounding workflow concerns solid powder collected into glass capsules. Thus, it supports an open-source software-controlled, calibrated powder dispensing system, but not a complete low-cost dispenser characterization or drug-stock preparation protocol.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides evidence for the biomimetic dual-arm dispenser as a non-commercial, relatively low-cost system capable of milligram-scale solid dispensing. It uses a highly dexterous dual-arm robotic manipulator, fuzzy-logic control, spatulas of various sizes, and an analytical balance to mimic manual weighing. The reported operating range extends from milligram to gram quantities, and experiments achieved dispensing accuracy as low as 2 mg, placing the system within the requested 1–5 mg accuracy range. A key operational feature is automatic reset and repeat dispensing when the sample exceeds a predefined tolerance. The authors suggest broad material compatibility, including solids that may abrade or block conventional dispensing units with moving parts, although highly deliquescent solids are identified as less compatible. contexts.context: For the Liver-Chip toxicology drug preparation, the excerpt does not specify a fixed starting powder mass. It states that powder drugs were weighed with 1 mg precision, or, alternatively, dissolved directly from the vendor-provided vial. No automated balance or automated weighing procedure is identified; the wording supports weighing by an operator, while the automated instrument mentioned elsewhere is a plate reader used for absorbance measurements. Sterile DMSO was used as the solvent. The dissolved material was triturated, transferred to an amber vial, and vortexed at high speed for 60 seconds to ensure complete dissolution. Serial dilutions in DMSO generated the subsequent 1000× stocks. Stocks were aliquoted into 1.5 mL tubes, stored at −20 °C, and allowed no more than one freeze-thaw cycle. On dosing day, a stock aliquot was thawed at 37 °C, vortexed, and checked for particulates. Dosing solutions were made by diluting the drug stock 1:1000 into either top or bottom media, producing 0.1% DMSO, then vortexed and held at 37 °C until dosing. The “ECHO” reference in this excerpt is explicitly the microscope used for brightfield imaging and morphology analysis, not an acoustic liquid dispenser.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports experiments on mixing DMSO drug-stock solutions with aqueous buffers, comparing no mixing, aspiration/dispense mixing, and vortex mixing across multiple laboratories and pipetting modes. It does not document solid dispensing, nanoliter liquid dispensing, organ-on-chip experiments, or the specific 2014 Griffith natural-product facility, 2019 manually prepared drug-combination stocks, or 2022 Liver Chip manually weighed drugs. The relevant finding is that the initial addition of organic and aqueous components was less influential than subsequent mixing. Manual and robotic pipetting produced no significant differences in supernatant drug amount or variability. In contrast, vigorous vortex mixing consistently reduced the amount of tolnaftate remaining in the supernatant, apparently by promoting nanoparticle growth, ripening, collisions, and aggregation, which increased particle removal during centrifugation. Nanoparticle tracking analysis supported this interpretation: before centrifugation, no-mix and vortex samples were similar, whereas after centrifugation vortex-mixed samples had fewer nanoparticles remaining in the supernatant. Thus, the excerpt may support a general point about solvent-mixing conditions affecting precipitated drug nanoparticles and assay variability, but it does not provide the requested explicit linkage to solid handling, nanoliter dispensing, or organ-on-chip workflows.

contexts.context: This 2016 study documents a compound-preparation experiment connecting solid-compound solubilization, solvent mixing, and low-volume liquid dispensing in an A549 mammalian cytotoxicity assay. Solid compounds were first solubilized in DMSO, transferred to an intermediate plate, and serially diluted. The original preparation used DMSO/water to control the final DMSO concentration, but some compounds precipitated after water addition, producing erratic IC50 values. The liquid-handling system was therefore optimized for submicroliter dispensing: serial dilutions were made in neat DMSO, and 0.5 µL of each diluted sample was stamped onto the assay plate. This volume corresponds to 500 nL, although the paper describes the method as low-volume dispensing rather than explicitly as nanoliter dispensing. The study reports no significant IC50 differences between 1 µL DMSO/water dispenses and 0.5 µL neat-DMSO dispenses for compounds without precipitation. It is not an organ-on-chip experiment, nor does it describe manually prepared drug-combination stocks or manually weighed drugs in a liver-chip system. Thus, it is relevant as a distinct 2016 automated compound-plate preparation and solvent/precipitation-control example, but it should not be conflated with the 2014 Griffith natural-product facility, 2019 manually prepared drug-combination stocks, or 2022 Liver Chip studies.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes STORMS as a stochastic, vacuum-assisted coring and glass-encapsulation workflow intended to decouple solid sampling from synthesis. It states that pre-calibrated sampling generates individually laser-sealed capsules, which are stored and later selected by a combinatorial matching algorithm before being broken over reaction vessels. The claimed demonstrated operating range is 0.1–20 mg across diverse solids, while the detailed calibration discussion reports two ranges, 0.1–1 mg and 1–8–10 mg, with the upper limit material-dependent and determined by the onset of nonlinearity. The method removes intermediate feedback weighing: only the empty-capsule and final capsule measurements are required. Dispensing variability is characterized using Gaussian distributions and linear regression; predefined tolerances are compensated during later liquid handling, including reagents, solutions, and solvents. This supports investigation of whether solvent volumes are adjusted to measured mass, but the excerpt does not specify the exact adjustment algorithm or provide numerical on-target error data. It also does not discuss hardware openness versus software, Miau’s $900 component-cost claim or validation at 1–5 mg, nor Winkler 2022 drug-stock loading details. The figures are referenced but not provided as usable images here.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general context relevant to evaluating STORMS, Miau, and prospective fluidic-chip systems, but it does not report primary data for any of those systems. It identifies accurate low-mass solid dispensing as an unresolved limitation to reliable closed-loop operation, directly framing the need for evidence of automated 1–5 mg capsule coring, mass accuracy, and solvent-volume adjustment based on measured mass. It also distinguishes hardware from the less-described software layer: orchestration software schedules and dispatches experiments, handles exceptions, and recovers from failures. Therefore, claims about hardware openness should be assessed separately from software openness and recoverability. The excerpt warns that practical autonomy is undermined by routine failures such as empty consumables, clogged syringes, and parser errors. contexts.context: The excerpt provides direct evidence that STORMS was engineered for automated solid coring across the 1–5 mg range: the specified 1.5 mm coring tube covers the broader 1–10 mg range, while the 0.6 mm tube covers 0.1–1 mg. Dispensed mass is controlled by the adjustable rod position, with vacuum assistance intended to improve filling reproducibility across powders and wax-like solids. Hardware details include interchangeable stainless-steel tubes and rods, robotic vial positioning, capsule dispensing, enclosed CO₂ laser sealing, and robotic capsule pick-and-place/crushing. Software is represented by calibration datasets, experimental mass tables, effective capsule distributions, and a rule-based matching algorithm that selects capsule combinations within a specified tolerance. Capsules are weighed after filling, so the system records the exact solid mass before storage and later reaction-plate assembly. However, this excerpt does not provide numerical on-target error, accuracy, or precision results for 1–5 mg dispensing, nor does it establish that solvent volume is automatically adjusted to measured mass. It also contains no information about Miau’s claimed $900 component cost or validation at 1–5 mg, and no details about Winkler 2022 drug-stock loading or a prospective minimal-fluidic chip.

It reports variable-volume transfers from a 384-well source plate, with reagent-specific additions ranging from 125 nL to 750 nL and a total reaction volume of 2.5 μL. contexts.context: The excerpt provides methodological evidence for automated solid microsampling and capsule weighing, but it does not directly establish all of the requested STORMS or Miau claims. The described UR3e robotic workflow retrieves an empty capsule, records its initial mass, cores powder using interchangeable 1.0 or 2.0 mm tube-and-rod assemblies, dispenses the powder into the capsule, and calculates sampled mass from the final-minus-initial weighing. The accompanying figure describes coring, vial shaking to remove the coring hole, dispensing, and final weighing. A separate calibration-and-dispensing software system dispenses and repeats measurements over a 1–9 mg range, fits a polynomial relating volume to delivered mass, and uses measured mass iteratively to reach a requested target within tolerance. This supports automated mass-based dispensing and calibration, but the excerpt does not report direct 1–5 mg capsule-coring results, quantitative on-target error, or automated solvent-volume adjustment based on measured mass. It also contains no component-cost information, so it cannot substantiate whether $900 is a true Miau component cost or whether that system was validated at 1–5 mg. No Winkler 2022 drug-stock loading details or prospective minimal-fluidic-chip information appear in the excerpt. Hardware/software openness is only partly documented through named hardware and a GitHub software repository.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides primary calibration and workflow evidence for STORMS, especially for milligram-scale capsule coring. Using a 1.5 mm vacuum-assisted coring tool, the authors report a linear relationship between rod height and dispensed mass across most tested powders; the 3–5 mg range is specifically favored by the matching algorithm to reduce relative balance uncertainty. For Inhalac 70, repeated measurements showed linear behavior from 1–6 mm rod height with R² = 0.9997, while dispersion remained stable throughout that range. The text attributes final precision to analytical-balance readability and repeatability, rather than describing a separate on-target error metric in the excerpt. It also states that vacuum-assisted sampling can broaden compatibility, particularly for larger particles and higher Carr-index powders. STORMS is described as an architecture combining pre-calibration, stochastic sampling, encapsulation, and algorithmic matching; the excerpt emphasizes workflow/software decoupling rather than hardware openness. Handling time is reported as 20–30 seconds per capsule versus approximately two minutes for deterministic dispensing, with substantial plate-level time reductions. No information here establishes automated solvent-volume adjustment based on measured capsule mass. The excerpt contains no data about Miau’s $900 component-cost claim or 1–5 mg validation, and no details about Winkler 2022 drug-stock loading for a prospective fluidic chip.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes low-cost automated **liquid**-handling and synthesis platforms, not solid-powder dispensing. Jubilee is modular, tool-changing, and can dispense liquids into 96-well plates; it was adapted for automated sonochemical nanocrystal synthesis. Caramelli et al. built replicable low-cost robots using peristaltic pumps, glass reaction vials, webcams, and pcDuino control for parallel chemical experiments. The Chemputer uses custom 3D-printed parts and syringe pumps but costs over $30,000; the mini-Chemputer reduces this to $10,000. No system here is reported dispensing 1–5 mg powders, automatically adding solvent/mixing, or feeding nanoliter/picoliter or organ-on-chip screening.

Symyx software controlled Powdernium dispensing, weighing, storage, solvent addition, whisk/shaker mixing, filtration, dilution, and UPLC analysis for **48 samples in parallel**, with mass tracking at every operation. contexts.context: This excerpt is a 2024 tutorial review on self-driving laboratories (SDLs), emphasizing modularity, reusable software classes, and low-cost automation. It states that “the same SOTA software” used on high-cost SDLs can run on low-cost systems, enabling rapid, low-risk prototyping and multi-fidelity experiments. It discusses human-inspired, hardware-centric, and human-in-the-loop designs, with examples involving needle wiping, peristaltic pumping, digitally controlled stirring, computer vision, and vial tracking using AprilTags. However, the excerpt provides no specific automated powder dispenser, milligram-scale solid dispensing, stock-solution preparation, or downstream nanoliter/microfluidic drug-screening implementation.

(2008) describe a commercial, integrated Symyx system—not low-cost/open-source—for automated solid handling. “Powdernium” dispenses drug/excipient into vials over a balance until a predetermined weight is reached; an XCM robot weighs each operation, stirs, stores, dissolves, filters, and dilutes samples before UPLC analysis. It fed UPLC, not nanoliter/picoliter dispensing or microfluidic/organ-on-chip screening.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a **commercial Labcyte Echo 550 acoustic liquid dispenser**, not a low-cost/open-source powder dispenser. Compounds were supplied as **10-mM DMSO stocks**, then serially diluted automatically to **100 µM, 1 µM, and 10 nM** using a Matrix Hydra liquid handler. contexts.context: A 2023 *Digital Discovery* paper reports a “relatively inexpensive” automated solid-dispensing platform based on an ABB YuMi dual-arm robot using human-like spatula operations. It compared the robot with Mettler-Toledo Quantos and Chemspeed systems across solids; average failure rates were 23.1%, 26.9%, and 26.5%, respectively. The robot handled many materials but failed with compressible CaCO₃ and hygroscopic ammonium acetate/potassium acetate. Codes, models, and results are openly available on GitHub. The authors propose connecting the modular station to vial transport and chemical-synthesis stations, but this excerpt reports no demonstrated 1–5 mg drug-stock preparation or nanoliter/microfluidic screening integration.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Wakasawa et al.’s compatibility-testing procedure for in-house compounds. Each test used 5 mg of compound with 0.5, 5, 45, or 50 mg of excipient in a 2-mL vial. Samples were manually vortex-mixed, then stored at 70 °C for 9 days to accelerate compound–excipient interactions. Dissolution used 1.0, 1.2, or 1.5 mL of solvent, selected according to compound-specific discovery-stage information. After dissolution, the suspension or solution was stirred and membrane-filtered, followed by dilution to compound-specific final concentrations of approximately 0.06–1.67 mg/mL; Drug C received an additional dilution. UPLC was the analytical endpoint, with compound-specific columns, temperatures, flow rates, injection volumes, and run times listed in Table 1. The excerpt does not explicitly identify Powdernium/XCM, robotic stirring or dilution, or a “non-ADE” endpoint; it specifically states that mixing was manual for these in-house-compound studies. Validation included dispensing and weighing, extraction, solution preparation, injection, and chromatographic analysis. With mass correction, conivaptan hydrochloride recoveries were 98.1–100.9% with RSDs of 1.3–2.3%; without correction, recoveries ranged from 93.5–108.1% with RSDs up to 6.2%, demonstrating the importance of unit-operation weighing and mass correction.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides practical context for preparing DMSO stock solutions and highlights important risks when converting weighed powder into concentrated stocks. It reports preparation of nominal 1 mM and 5 mM individual-compound stocks in DMSO, with actual concentrations ranging from 0.99–1.03 mM and 4.97–5.08 mM, demonstrating that nominal concentrations should be checked against the accurately weighed mass and final volume. For a compound with molecular weight 500 g/mol, a 10 mM stock corresponds to 5 g/L, or 5 mg/mL; therefore, 1 mg would require 200 μL of DMSO, while 1–5 mg would require approximately 200–1000 μL. The excerpt does not discuss acoustic dispensing at 2.5 nL, microfluidic organ-chip DMSO tolerance, or powder-weighing error quantitatively. However, it strongly supports caution about precipitation after DMSO stocks are mixed with aqueous buffers: hydrophobic screening compounds may precipitate, forming nanoparticles whose size and concentration change over time. Protein can slow nanoparticle formation and ripening, and adding protein after precipitation begins may reduce interactions. These effects should be considered when selecting stock concentration, dilution volume, and downstream assay timing.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides a practical DMSO-d6 stock-preparation framework that can be adapted to powder quantities in the 1–5 mg range. Its worked procedure targets a 20 mM stock, using an exact-mass/molecular-weight calculation to determine the DMSO volume, and begins with 0.3–0.6 mg of compound. contexts.context: The excerpt supports caution when preparing DMSO stock solutions of poorly water-soluble compounds and subsequently diluting them into aqueous systems. It states that discovery compounds are commonly stored dissolved in DMSO, while most drug molecules are largely water insoluble. The reported experiments show that precipitation and particle growth after mixing can be slow and may continue over several hours, so an apparently clear mixture immediately after dilution may not remain clear. NanoSight detected the emergence of a polydisperse particle distribution over time, whereas DLS primarily showed an increase in mean particle diameter and was biased toward larger, more strongly scattering particles. These findings are relevant to downstream screening workflows because precipitated material can affect assay results and particle measurements. contexts.context: The excerpt is relevant to the requested practical workflow mainly because it cautions that compounds transferred from DMSO stocks into aqueous buffers can precipitate or form colloidal aggregates. It defines kinetic solubility assays as measurements beginning with DMSO stock solutions and distinguishes kinetic solubility from thermodynamic solubility: kinetic solubility reflects the maximum concentration of the fastest-precipitating form, whereas thermodynamic solubility concerns the most stable form. The discussion emphasizes that apparent nanoparticle or aggregate dissolution after dilution does not rule out precipitation; small particles may dissolve rapidly because of their high surface area. Hydrophobicity, solubility, and clogP can help predict aggregation, but are not fully definitive. Lowering assay concentrations may reduce aggregation. However, the excerpt does not provide the requested numerical preparation examples for 1–5 mg powders, a 500 g/mol molecular weight, 10 mM DMSO stocks, or the calculation that 1 mg requires 200 µL. contexts.context: The excerpt supports preparing compounds as 10 mM DMSO stocks and then removing or diluting the DMSO before downstream testing. For a compound with molecular weight 500 g/mol, 1 mg corresponds to 2 µmol; at 10 mM, this requires 200 µL of DMSO. Accordingly, practical examples are 1 mg in 200 µL, 2 mg in 400 µL, 3 mg in 600 µL, 4 mg in 800 µL, and 5 mg in 1.00 mL. These stock volumes can be used for very-low-volume acoustic dispensing, including 2.5 nL transfers, provided the stock is homogeneous and the delivery system is compatible with DMSO. For microfluidic organ-chip applications, the excerpt emphasizes controlling residual DMSO rather than relying on the nominal stock concentration: the reported protocol used mild evaporation for approximately 60 minutes and found no noticeable DMSO contribution in a representative solubility sample, with a DMSO quantification limit of 0.025%. If evaporation is not used, the final DMSO percentage should be calculated against the organ chip’s validated tolerance. Practical handling cautions include incomplete dissolution or precipitation at the chosen stock concentration, adsorption or sample loss, and powder-weighing error, especially for 1 mg-scale preparations. Verify clarity, mix thoroughly, and prepare excess stock when feasible.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports practical caution when preparing small quantities of powder for DMSO-based solubility workflows. It notes that conventional equilibrium-solubility testing may require multiple individually weighed samples and approximately 4–5 mg of compound, whereas the miniaturized protocol uses about 0.6 mg. For a compound with molecular weight 500 g/mol, 1 mg contains 2 µmol; a 10 mM solution therefore requires 200 µL, so 1–5 mg corresponds to approximately 200–1000 µL at that concentration. The excerpt does not specifically discuss 2.5 nL acoustic transfer, microfluidic organ-chip DMSO tolerance, or powder weighing error, but those downstream constraints make accurate stock preparation especially important. Residual DMSO can artificially increase measured aqueous equilibrium solubility, producing false-positive results; even 1–2% DMSO may increase values one- to threefold, while low-solubility compounds can show much larger increases. The authors therefore recommend performing dissolution and incubation without DMSO when preserving equilibrium-solubility integrity. In practice, precipitation during dilution or transfer should be checked, and weighing uncertainty becomes proportionally significant at the 1 mg scale.

It states that DMSO stocks are commonly stored at 10–30 mM, while another recommendation identifies 2–5 mM as an optimum concentration for reducing precipitation risk. contexts.context: The excerpt provides general context about miniaturized drug-discovery platforms but does not identify or describe the specific Winkler et al. (2022) Raspberry Pi, servo-operated, 3D-printed microfluidic micromixer, nor does it report the camptothecin preparation, drug concentration, volumes, IC50 assay format, or whether the biological test used an on-chip organ model versus a conventional plate. It states that miniaturized systems commonly use automated liquid handling, reaction blocks with agitation and temperature control, and 96-, 384-, or 1536-well plate reactors operating at micro- to nanoliter scale. The article also distinguishes manual miniaturized chemistry from automated systems and notes that gravimetric solid dispensing can deliver sub-milligram quantities of catalytic powders. However, this passage does not establish that the Winkler device used upstream automated powder dispensing; the cited powder examples are generic platform capabilities (palladium catalyst and Cs2CO3), not evidence about the Winkler workflow. Likewise, the mention of biological screening and destination microplates is a general description and cannot confirm the assay’s specific hardware or sample volumes.
contexts.question: Winkler et al. 2022 open-script Raspberry Pi servo-operated 3D printed microfluidic micromixer camptothecin IC50 assay: what drug preparation and volumes, does it actually use on-chip organ vs plate, and any upstream automated powder dispensing?

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone built or used a low-cost or open-source automated powder dispenser (gravimetric, auger, vibratory or tapping) to prepare drug or compound stock solutions, i.e. dispensing roughly 1-5 mg of solid into a vial followed by automated solvent addition and mixing, that then feed a downstream nanoliter/picoliter liquid dispenser or a microfluidic / lab-on-a-chip / organ-on-chip drug screening device?

No. ## Short answer

**Yes, closely related workflows have been built, but I did not find a published demonstration satisfying every condition at once:** a **low-cost or open-source** dispenser delivering **1–5 mg of an ordinary drug powder** into a vial, followed by **automated solvent addition and mixing**, with that newly prepared stock feeding a **nanoliter/picoliter liquid dispenser or drug-screening chip**. The strongest precedents establish different portions of that chain; they should not be described as one validated, inexpensive end-to-end system. (wakasawa2008solidstatecompatibilitystudies pages 2-4, wakasawa2008solidstatecompatibilitystudies pages 4-5, butler2014naturalproductlibraries pages 4-5, shinn2019highthroughputscreeningfor pages 4-9, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 9-13)

| Published example | What was demonstrated | Where it falls short of the proposed system |
|---|---|---|
| **Astellas Powdernium/XCM, 2008 — closest match for the 5-mg preparation step.** | A commercial robot dispensed and weighed drug and excipient into glass vials; its companion workstation added solvent, stirred, filtered, diluted and tracked mass. One experiment dispensed **5 mg of an in-house compound into a 2-mL vial**, then used **1–1.5 mL solvent**. | This was a pharmaceutical compatibility/analytical workflow ending in **UPLC**, not acoustic dispensing or chip screening. Vial racks were transferred manually, and the cited 5-mg experiments specify **manual vortex mixing** before storage; it is not a fully unattended example or a low-cost/open-source build. (wakasawa2008solidstatecompatibilitystudies pages 1-2, wakasawa2008solidstatecompatibilitystudies pages 2-4, wakasawa2008solidstatecompatibilitystudies pages 4-5) |
| **Queensland Compound Library, described in 2014 — closest connection to acoustic screening.** | Barcoded samples were tracked from an **automated weighing station**, dissolved in dry DMSO, and subsequently transferred by an **acoustic dispenser** into screening microplates. | The description does not establish a **1–5 mg** dose, identify an inexpensive/open-source weighing mechanism, or explicitly say that **solvent addition and mixing** were automated. The endpoint was screening plates, not an organ-on-chip. (butler2014naturalproductlibraries pages 4-5) |
| **STORMS, 2026 — closest disclosed milligram-scale solid-handling architecture.** | Robotic **vacuum-assisted coring** fills individually weighed, sealable glass capsules. Its milligram coring tool covers approximately **1–10 mg**, and the authors highlight **3–5 mg** portions; calibration and capsule-selection software are publicly referenced. Capsules can subsequently be opened over reaction vessels. | It uses a robot, balance and laser-sealing apparatus; **open software is not evidence of low-cost or entirely open hardware**. The reported work does not demonstrate DMSO stock preparation followed by acoustic dispensing or biological chip screening. It is coring, not an auger, vibratory or tapping feeder. (lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 9-13, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 18-21, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 13-15) |
| **Miau Microbalance Autosampler — inexpensive solid-handling precedent.** | A review lists a roughly **US$900**, 3D-printed pick-and-place device that transfers tin capsules and powder for **sub-milligram** analytical samples. | Its documented application is elemental/isotope sample preparation; the reviewed description does **not validate 1–5 mg drug dosing**, solvent addition, or downstream screening. Its original *HardwareX* paper was not available for direct verification in this search. (doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 18-19, doloi2025democratizingselfdrivinglabs pages 19-20) |
| **Dual-arm biomimetic dispenser, 2023 — reusable robot-controlled weighing.** | Published code accompanies an ABB YuMi robot that manipulates spatulas, vials and a balance; its illustrated sequence shows solid delivery into vials. | Its stated **minimum dose is 20 ± 2 mg**: the **2 mg is a tolerance around 20 mg, not evidence of a 2-mg target**. The authors call it relatively inexpensive compared with commercial systems but give no demonstrated 1–5 mg drug-stock-to-screen workflow. (jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 2-3, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid pages 10-11, jiang2023autonomousbiomimeticsolid media baa5662d) |

**What happens downstream is well established, but usually starts with an already prepared stock.** In an NCATS drug-combination-screening protocol, investigators first *weighed compound into a tube* to make **800 µL of 10 mM DMSO stock**, vortexed and checked dissolution; automation then prepared acoustic source plates and used an ATS-100 dispenser. That is a direct precedent for the liquid-screening half, **not automated initial powder weighing**. Separately, an Echo 550 cell-screening study dispensed **2.5–100 nL** from DMSO source plates. (shinn2019highthroughputscreeningfor pages 4-9, shinn2019highthroughputscreeningfor pages 1-4, grant2009achievingaccuratecompound pages 2-3)

**For a microfluidic endpoint**, a relatively low-cost, 3D-printed, Raspberry-Pi-controlled valve/micromixer has delivered premade camptothecin solutions to cell-culture wells for an IC₅₀ assay. Its demonstrated cells were in a **conventional plate**, not an organ cultured on-chip; powder-to-stock preparation was not automated. A human Liver-Chip study similarly prepared drug stocks from weighed powder or vendor vials and diluted them into perfusion medium, but did not report automated powder dispensing. Its reference to an “ECHO” instrument means an **imaging microscope**, not an Echo acoustic dispenser. (winkler2022automationofcell pages 1-2, winkler2022automationofcell pages 4-5, winkler2022automationofcell media 4dcdf57f, ewart2022performanceassessmentand pages 4-5, ewart2022performanceassessmentand pages 3-4)

**Practical interpretation.** The proposed integration is technically plausible, but its missing demonstration is the *validated interface* between an affordable 1–5 mg powder dispenser and automated, concentration-controlled stock production. Actual dispensed mass—not just the requested mass—should determine solvent volume; dissolution, precipitation after aqueous dilution, and compatibility with the destination assay need checking. For scale, **1 mg of a 500 g/mol compound requires 200 µL solvent for a nominal 10 mM stock**, while 5 mg requires 1 mL; this is a calculation, not a claim that any cited dispenser validated those stocks. The Astellas study illustrates why mass tracking matters: at its 5-mg validation point, mass-corrected recovery was **100.9%** versus **108.1%** without correction. (wakasawa2008solidstatecompatibilitystudies pages 4-5, laplante2021probingthefreestate pages 98-102, gillespie2013theprecipitationof pages 70-76)

**Bottom line:** *Yes* to automated ~5-mg drug dispensing followed by solvent processing, and *yes* to automated weighing followed eventually by acoustic screening **as separate published precedents**. *No verified example found* of their requested **low-cost/open-source, 1–5 mg, fully connected powder-to-stock-to-nanoliter-dispenser or organ-chip implementation**. (wakasawa2008solidstatecompatibilitystudies pages 2-4, wakasawa2008solidstatecompatibilitystudies pages 4-5, butler2014naturalproductlibraries pages 4-5, shinn2019highthroughputscreeningfor pages 4-9, lisowski2026highthroughputsolidmicrosampling pages 9-13)

info.query: Has anyone built or used a low-cost or open-source automated powder dispenser (gravimetric, auger, vibratory or tapping) to prepare drug or compound stock solutions, i.e. dispensing roughly 1-5 mg of solid into a vial followed by automated solvent addition and mixing, that then feed a downstream nanoliter/picoliter liquid dispenser or a microfluidic / lab-on-a-chip / organ-on-chip drug screening device?
